title: Unraveling the nexus: Tumor mutational burden, PD‐L1 expression, and oncogenic alterations in non–small cell lung cancer cytology specimens
author: Min Dai; Francis Anthony San Lucas; Hector Alvarez; Leomar Ballester; Hui Chen; Keyur P Patel; Asif Rashid; Shun Rao; Mark J Routbort; Gloria Sura; Keith Sweeney; Gokce Toruner; Peng Wei; Richard Yang; Hyvan Dang; Rajyalakshmi Luthra; Sinchita Roy‐Chowdhuri
text:
Abstract
Background
PD‐L1 expression and tumor mutational burden (TMB) are biomarkers for immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) therapy in non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC); however, patients harboring oncogenic alterations have limited benefit from ICIs. The impact of oncogenic alterations on TMB and PD‐L1 tumor proportion score in lung cytology specimens is poorly understood. Herein, the association between oncogenic alterations, TMB, and PD‐L1 in NSCLC cytology specimens is explored.
Methods
Next‐generation sequencing results from 312 NSCLC cytology specimens were retrospectively reviewed that interrogate 610 genes and select immuno‐oncology signatures. TMB and PD‐L1 immunohistochemical expression across oncogenic alterations were analyzed to explore associations.
Results
Of the 312 cases evaluated, 192 harbored NSCLC‐specific oncogenic alterations. Relative to EGFR‐mutated tumors, TMB was significantly higher in KRAS (p adj = 2.7 × 10−4), ERBB2 (p adj = .023), and BRAF (p adj = .023) ‐mutated tumors but lower in ALK‐rearranged tumors (p adj = .005). Significantly higher PD‐L1 expression was seen in tumors with KRAS (p adj = .002) and MET exon 14 (p adj = 1.06 × 10−4) when compared to EGFR‐mutated tumors. Strong positive correlations between TMB and PD‐L1 were observed in ERBB2‐, KRAS‐, and BRAF‐mutated tumors when evaluated as continuous variables. TP53 mutations further enhanced immunogenicity when co‐occurring with KRAS, ERBB2, or BRAF mutations but this effect was not observed in EGFR‐mutated tumors.
Conclusions
These findings demonstrate distinct TMB and PD‐L1 profiles that may identify patients who will benefit from ICI therapy. Cytology specimens provide adequate material for biomarker testing, which underscores their value in guiding immunotherapy decisions.
Keywords: cytology, immuno‐oncology, next‐generation sequencing, non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), PD‐L1, tumor mutational burden (TMB)
Short abstract
PD‐L1 expression and tumor mutational burden (TMB) are biomarkers for immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) therapy in non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC); however, patients harboring oncogenic alterations have limited benefit from ICIs. Herein, the association between oncogenic alterations, TMB, and PD‐L1 in NSCLC cytology specimens is explored. These findings demonstrate distinct TMB and PD‐L1 profiles that may identify patients who will benefit from ICI therapy. Cytology specimens provide adequate material for biomarker testing, which underscores their value in guiding immunotherapy decisions.
INTRODUCTION
Lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer‐related mortality worldwide by accounting for the highest number of cancer deaths among both men and women. 1 In the past decade, rapid progress in immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) therapies that block proteins such as PD‐1 and PD‐L1 has greatly improved outcomes in patients with advanced non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). 2 , 3 , 4 Several ICI agents, such as pembrolizumab, nivolumab, atezolizumab, and durvalumab, have shown improved survival rates compared to traditional chemotherapy, and are now standard first‐line treatment, either alone or with chemotherapy, especially in advanced or metastatic disease. For patients with high PD‐L1 expression (≥50%), single‐agent immunotherapy can sometimes replace chemotherapy as first‐line treatment. Despite these advances, only approximately 20%–25% of patients with NSCLC derive sustained clinical benefit from ICI therapy. The mechanisms underlying the limited efficacy of ICIs are still unclear, with contributing factors likely including tumor‐intrinsic features, host immune responses, and activation of resistance pathways.
Tumor mutational burden (TMB) measures the total number of somatic mutations per megabase (mut/Mb) of tumor DNA; tumors with a higher TMB likely have more tumor‐specific neoantigens, which increases the chance of response to ICIs. 5 Early studies, such as CheckMate 227, 6 suggested that patients with high TMB (≥10 mut/Mb) treated with nivolumab plus ipilimumab had better progression‐free survival compared to chemotherapy. In 2020, on the basis of results from KEYNOTE‐158, 7 the Food and Drug Administration granted accelerated approval of pembrolizumab for patients with tumors with high TMB (≥10 mut/Mb) who have progressed after prior treatment and are without any satisfactory alternative treatment options. However, later studies have suggested that although high TMB can correlate with improved response rates, it does not consistently predict overall survival benefit. 8
Targeted therapies directed against oncogenic drivers such as EGFR and ALK alterations have markedly extended survival in patients with NSCLC who harbor these alterations. 9 However, resistance to these agents is nearly universal, and durable remissions remain rare. Furthermore, patients with targetable oncogenic alterations often respond poorly to ICI therapy, 10 , 11 which highlights the importance of appropriate patient selection to minimize immune‐related adverse events and optimize therapeutic benefit. The impact of specific oncogenic alterations on TMB and PD‐L1 expression, the established predictive biomarkers of ICI therapy, remains incompletely understood. Therefore, understanding how driver mutations influence the tumor immune microenvironment may help refine treatment strategies and expand the clinical utility of immunotherapy in NSCLC.
Most studies to date have been conducted on formalin‐fixed, paraffin‐embedded (FFPE) histology specimens. However, cytology samples—often obtained via less invasive procedures and accounting for up to 30% of NSCLC specimens—can provide high‐quality genomic material from non‐FFPE cytology preparations that are suitable for molecular analysis. In many cases, especially in advanced NSCLC, cytology specimens may be the only available material for diagnosis and molecular testing. Several studies have demonstrated that next‐generation sequencing (NGS) can be successfully applied to various cytology preparations, 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 including smears and cell blocks. Furthermore, clinical practice guidelines from the College of American Pathologists recommend the use of cytology specimens for molecular analysis in patients with NSCLC. 16 , 17 Nevertheless, the use of cytology specimens for NGS remains limited largely because of the underutilization of diverse preparation techniques and insufficient validation of assays across different cytology formats. 18 , 19
To address this knowledge gap, we conducted a retrospective analysis of NSCLC cytology specimens via NGS to evaluate the association between oncogenic alterations, TMB, and PD‐L1 expression. Our goal was to evaluate the feasibility of cytology specimen preparations to define distinct immunogenomic profiles that could inform more precise, biomarker‐driven approaches to immunotherapy in NSCLC.
MATERIALS AND METHODS
Patient samples
A retrospective review of all cytology specimens with a diagnosis of NSCLC that were evaluated by NGS at our institution between January 2020 and December 2022 was included in this study. Routine FFPE tissue from fine‐needle aspiration cell block and cytology smear preparations, as well as Diff‐Quik– and Papanicolaou‐stained samples, were used in this study. Specimen adequacy for NGS was defined as a tumor fraction of ≥20% that met the specimen requirements of our molecular diagnostics laboratory. Hematoxylin–eosin–stained cell block sections and stained cytology direct smears were reviewed, tumor‐rich areas were demarcated, and nucleic acid extraction was performed by scraping circled, tumor‐mapped areas by macrodissection or manual microdissection under light microscopy.
NGS
Nucleic acids from cytology specimens were extracted with the AllPrep DNA/RNA Extraction Kit (Qiagen) and/or a PicoPure DNA Extraction Kit (Thermo Fisher), as previously described. 14 , 20 Genomic alterations were determined with the MD Anderson Mutation Analysis Precision Panel (MDA MAPP), which is a custom hybridization capture–based NGS assay that interrogates mutations in 610 genes, select gene fusions, copy number alterations, microsatellite instability status, and TMB. MDA MAPP uses DNA extracted from both tumor tissue and paired normal (peripheral blood or tissue) specimens in our Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments–certified molecular diagnostics laboratory to facilitate analysis of variants that are of somatic origin. Specimen requirement criteria included a minimum of 20% tumor cellularity with a DNA input of 46.4 ng. Thresholds for library preparation and sequencing were set as follows: tumor libraries ≥ 500 ng; total yield of target enriched DNA libraries ≥ 2.2 nM; quality score ≥ 70%; number of molecule reads ≥ 14 million; median consensus read coverage ≥ 200; on‐target rate of raw reads ≥ 40%; and percentage target above 100× ≥ 90%. TMB was determined by measuring the number of somatic mutations occurring in sequenced genes, and specified as a rate (mut/Mb). High TMB was defined as ≥10 mut/Mb.
Furthermore, an RNA‐based NGS assay was used to detect oncogenic fusions. Complementary DNA prepared from extracted RNA was combined with targeted amplicon‐based NGS to amplify both a set of expected control RNA sequences and a set of targeted fusion sequences corresponding to clinically relevant known inter‐ and intragenic fusions in 51 genes.
PD‐L1 staining
Cell blocks from the cytology specimens were used for PD‐L1 testing via immunohistochemistry (IHC) with the 22C3 pharmDx assay (Dako North America). PD‐L1 expression was quantified as the tumor proportion score (TPS), and defined as negative (<1%), low expression (1%–49%), or high expression (≥50%). The PD‐L1 TPS, which was evaluated in the clinical diagnostic setting, was retrospectively obtained from pathology reports.
Statistical analysis
TMB and PD‐L1 expression were analyzed across oncogenic alteration subgroups to evaluate mutual associations via nonparametric methods for subgroup comparisons. A Kruskal–Wallis test was used to assess global difference across subgroups, and pairwise Mann–Whitney U tests were performed comparing each subgroup to the EGFR‐mutated group that served as a reference. To assess the association between TMB and PD‐L1, both categorical and continuous analyses were conducted. For categorical analysis, TMB and PD‐L1 were dichotomized at ≥10 mut/Mb (high TMB) and ≥50% (high expressors), respectively, and analyzed with either a χ2 test or Fisher exact test. Odds ratios and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) are reported with both inferential and continuity‐corrected estimates. For continuous analysis, the Spearman rank correlation test was applied within each oncogenic subgroup. Both forest plots and scatterplots with regression lines (for significant associations) were generated for visualization. All analyses were performed with R (version 4.2.1). Tests were two sided, with a significance level of .05. For families of multiple comparisons, Benjamini–Hochberg adjustment was used to control the false discovery rate (FDR) and ensure that only results remaining significant after the adjustment were interpreted as true differences. Details of the statistical analysis are included in Supplementary Material.
RESULTS
Patient demographics and specimen characteristics
We evaluated the biomarker test results from 312 NSCLC cytology specimens, including DNA‐ and RNA‐based NGS analysis and PD‐L1 IHC. Patient median age was 70 years (range, 41–97 years), with a slight female preponderance (female, 159; male, 153). Adenocarcinoma was the most prevalent cytology subtype, observed in 74.4% of cases (232 of 312), followed by squamous cell carcinoma in 13.1% (41 of 312) and NSCLC, not otherwise specified in 12.5% (39 of 312). The clinical and pathological characteristics of the patients evaluated are summarized in Table 1. The specimen preparations used for testing included cell blocks (n = 150; 48.1%), direct smears (n = 113; 36.2%), and a combination of smears and cell block sections (n = 49; 15.7%).

Oncogene‐addicted NSCLCs exhibit distinct patterns of TMB
Of the 312 cases evaluated, 192 (61.5%) harbored clinically relevant oncogenic alterations in EGFR, KRAS, BRAF, ERBB2, ALK, RET, ROS1, and MET exon 14. Kruskal–Wallis analysis revealed significant global heterogeneity in TMB across the various oncogenic alterations (χ = 39.255; df, 6; p = 6.38 × 10−7). In comparison to EGFR‐mutated tumors (median TMB, 4.08 mut/Mb), a significantly higher TMB was seen in tumors harboring KRAS (median, 7.24; p adj = 2.7 × 10−4), ERBB2 (median, 10.28; p adj = .023), and BRAF mutations (median, 8.14; p adj = .023), whereas a significantly lower TMB was seen in tumors harboring alterations in ALK (median, 1.92; p adj = .005). In contrast, TMB in tumors with alterations in MET exon 14 (median, 6.69; p adj = .058) and RET genes (median, 1.81; p adj = .083) was not statistically significant after adjustment for multiple comparisons (Table 2; Figure 1). Within tumors harboring a KRAS mutation, no significant difference in TMB was found in tumors harboring a p.G12C mutation (n = 24) compared with tumors harboring a non‐G12C mutation (n = 52). Also, within tumors harboring a BRAF mutation, no significant difference in TMB was found in tumors harboring a p.V600E mutation (n = 5) compared with tumors harboring a non‐V600E mutation (n = 16). Comparison of TMB between samples tested from direct smears versus those from cell block preparations did not show any statistical difference (p = .27).

Oncogene‐addicted NSCLCs exhibit distinct patterns of PD‐L1 expression
PD‐L1 expression was analyzed in NSCLC cases with relevant oncogenic alterations. PD‐L1 IHC testing was available for 177 of the 192 cases, and showed significant global heterogeneity (χ2 = 26.352; df, 6; p = 1.92 × 10−4). Relative to EGFR‐mutated tumors (median TPS, 5), significantly higher PD‐L1 expression was seen in tumors with KRAS mutations (median TPS, 15; p adj = .002) and MET exon 14 alterations (median TPS, 55; p adj = 1.06 × 10−4) (Figure 2). There was no significant difference in PD‐L1 expression after multiplicity adjustment in tumors harboring ERBB2 mutations (median TPS, 45; p adj = .064), BRAF mutations (median TPS, 5; p adj = .387), and fusions in ALK (median TPS, 7.5; p adj = .623) and RET genes (median TPS, 0; p adj = .623). No significant difference in PD‐L1 expression level was found between tumors with a KRAS p.G12C mutation (n = 24) and tumors harboring a non‐G12C mutation (n = 52), or between tumors harboring a BRAF p.V600E mutation (n = 5) and tumors harboring a non‐V600E mutation (n = 16).
Furthermore, high PD‐L1 expression (TPS, ≥50%) was more frequently reported in tumors harboring KRAS (28 of 72; 38.9%), ERBB2 (five of 10; 50%), BRAF (seven of 21; 33.3%), or MET exon 14 skipping alterations (seven of 10; 70%) when compared with tumors with an EGFR mutation (five of 48; 10.4%), ALK fusion (one of eight; 12.5%), or RET fusion (one of seven; 14.3%) (Figure S1).
High TMB and PD‐L1 expression are associated with specific oncogenic alterations
Categorical analyses of tumors with oncogenic alterations with high TMB (≥10 mut/Mb) and high PD‐L1 expression (TPS, ≥50%) did not show any statistically significant association, with variable distributions of PD‐L1 versus TMB within each alteration (Figure S2). ERBB2‐mutated tumors displayed a strong trend toward concurrent high TMB and high PD‐L1 expression (Fisher exact test, p = .0079; p adj = .056) (Figure 3). In contrast, a continuous association analysis suggested that the association between TMB and PD‐L1 expression is gene specific—strongest in ERBB2‐mutated tumors (p = .83; p adj = .024) and to a lesser degree in tumors with KRAS (p = .32; p adj = .030) and BRAF mutations (p = .54; p adj = .032). This implies a trend where tumors with a higher TMB may also express higher PD‐L1 expression (Figure 4). Linear slope estimates did not remain significant after FDR adjustment, except for ERBB2‐mutated tumors that demonstrated a significant association (p adj < .05), demonstrated by the positive regression slope (β = 5.82; 95% CI, 2.20–9.43) (Figure 5). Tumors with alterations in EGFR, ALK, MET exon 14, RET, and TP53 showed little to no evidence of correlation.
TP53 mutations enhance TMB and PD‐L1 expression in oncogene‐addicted NSCLCs
In our cohort, 196 cases (63%) harbored TP53 mutations, either alone (n = 61) or in conjunction (n = 135) with NSCLC‐relevant oncogenic alterations. Tumors with TP53 mutations in conjunction with other oncogenic alterations tended to have a higher TMB than tumors with an EGFR mutation, KRAS mutation, ALK fusion, or RET fusion alone. Notably, tumors with concurrent TP53 mutations with ERBB2, KRAS, BRAF, or MET exon 14 skipping mutations were associated with higher TMB and PD‐L1 expression compared to tumors with ERBB2, KRAS, or BRAF mutations only. TP53‐mutated tumors demonstrated a significantly higher TMB compared to EGFR‐mutated tumors without concurrent TP53 alterations (median, 8.54 vs. 4.10; p adj = .029). No significant difference in PD‐L1 expression was observed between TP53‐mutated tumors and EGFR‐mutated tumors without TP53 comutation (median TPS, 10 vs. 5; p adj = .187).
DISCUSSION
The therapeutic landscape for NSCLC has evolved over the past few decades, driven by the rapid development of targeted therapies and immunotherapies. Patients with advanced NSCLC require biomarker testing to help guide treatment decisions. Recent updates from the National Comprehensive Cancer Network and American Society of Clinical Oncology recommend ICI therapy as a first‐line option for patients with PD‐L1 expression of ≥50%, and combination chemoimmunotherapy for those with PD‐L1 expression of ≥1%. 21 , 22 Although immunotherapy offers promising clinical benefits in many patients with advanced NSCLC, its efficacy is limited in those harboring targetable oncogenic alterations. 23 , 24 The role of ICIs in this subset remains controversial, given that emerging evidence suggests that driver mutations are associated with distinct immune microenvironments and variable biomarker profiles, including PD‐L1 expression and TMB. 25
Consistent with prior reports, our study confirms that patients with NSCLC with alterations in EGFR and ALK genes exhibit low PD‐L1 expression and TMB, which would correlate with low response to ICIs. 26 , 27 In contrast, studies have reported that patients with NSCLC with KRAS, BRAF non‐V600E, or MET exon 14 alterations demonstrate higher PD‐L1 expression and elevated TMB, which suggests enhanced immunogenicity and greater responsiveness to immunotherapy. 10 , 28 , 29 Our study performed on a cohort of NSCLC cytology specimens supports findings from these prior studies. KRAS‐ and BRAF‐mutated tumors in our cohort showed elevated PD‐L1 and TMB, whereas EGFR‐, ALK‐, and RET‐altered tumors were associated with a “cold” immune phenotype marked by lower PD‐L1 expression and TMB. Interestingly, our data revealed a significant positive monotonic correlation between TMB and PD‐L1 expression in ERBB2‐mutated NSCLC cases, which suggests that tumors with ERBB2 mutations and a higher mutational load also tend to have higher PD‐L1 expression. Larger studies are warranted to clarify the immune characteristics of ERBB2‐mutated tumors.
TP53, a well‐known tumor suppressor gene, has been historically associated with adverse clinical outcomes and chemotherapy resistance. Recent data suggest that TP53 mutations may be associated with higher TMB and PD‐L1 expression. 30 , 31 , 32 Our results indicate that NSCLC tumors harboring TP53 mutations have higher PD‐L1 expression and TMB. Moreover, tumors harboring concurrent TP53 mutations with KRAS, ERBB2, or BRAF mutations displayed higher biomarker levels than tumors with individual mutations alone, which suggests that TP53 may modulate the immunogenicity of oncogene‐driven NSCLC. Notably, this effect was not observed in EGFR‐mutated tumors, which further underscores the unique immune landscape of EGFR‐driven NSCLC, which may involve mechanisms of immune evasion that extend beyond mutational load. Prior studies 26 , 33 , 34 have also reported EGFR‐mutated NSCLC tumors to have lower numbers of cytotoxic T cells, low T cell–receptor clonality, increased signaling in TGF‐β and adenosine pathways, and lower IFN‐γ expression, which are suggestive of other underlying mechanisms that contribute to the cold immune microenvironment in EGFR‐mutated tumors.
As mentioned previously, the literature on immuno‐oncology profiling of cytology NSCLC specimens is limited. A few studies 35 , 36 , 37 have reported the feasibility of evaluating TMB on cytology specimens. In this study, we provide data from a cohort of NSCLC cytology specimens, and report on the feasibility of determining immuno‐oncology therapeutic decisions on the basis of the patient’s genomic profile, PD‐L1 expression, and TMB. Among the 312 cases, cell blocks were used for 150 cases (48.1%), smear slides were used for 113 cases (36.2%), and a combination of cell blocks and smear slides was used for the remaining 49 cases (15.7%). Previous studies have primarily relied on FFPE histologic samples. However, cytology specimens often represent the only available material available for diagnosis and biomarker testing in advanced‐stage NSCLC. 38 Our findings demonstrate that NGS can be reliably performed on cytology preparations—including cell blocks and direct smears—and yield high‐quality DNA and RNA suitable for detailed genomic and immuno‐oncology profiling. 13 , 20
Despite the promising results, our study has several limitations. First, the sample size is relatively small for drawing definitive conclusions across the heterogeneous NSCLC population. Second, certain risk factors, such as smoking status, that are known to drive specific oncogenic alterations 39 , 40 were not available for analysis in our study cohort. For instance, a study by Sun et al. reported an increase in TP53, KRAS, and PIK3 gene mutations in patients with a smoking history compared with nonsmoking patients, and the TMB value in patients with lung adenocarcinoma correlated with the smoking index (pack × year). 41 Further studies are needed to explore whether smoking status/history correlates with the TMB differences seen in specific oncogenic populations. Third, cytology specimens are inherently subject to preanalytical variables that may affect the quality and consistency of downstream testing. 42 Factors such as fixation methods, staining protocols, and slide preparation techniques can influence the integrity of nucleic acids and protein epitopes, and potentially affect the performance of IHC (such as PD‐L1 assessment) and NGS testing. 43 , 44 Moreover, the retrospective nature of the study may introduce bias or limit the generalizability of the findings. The cytology specimens included in this study cohort met all set criteria for specimen requirements (tumor cellularity, DNA yield, and sequencing metrics). Although a comparison of TMB values from our study cohort with those obtained from surgical pathology resections would provide further data for the performance of TMB assessment from cytology samples, such an analysis was beyond the scope of this article. Future prospective studies with standardized protocols and larger, more diverse cohorts are needed to validate and expand upon these observations.
Taken together, our study underscores the clinical utility of integrating molecular and immune biomarker testing—especially in cytology specimens—for guiding immunotherapy decisions in NSCLC. Our findings highlight the distinct immunogenomic profiles associated with specific oncogenic alterations in NSCLC, and emphasize the importance of biomarker stratification when considering ICI therapy. These results also reinforce previous reports that oncogene status substantially influences PD‐L1 expression and TMB, which in turn affect immunotherapy responsiveness. Future research should focus on validating these findings in larger, prospective cohorts and exploring novel combination strategies that pair ICIs with targeted therapies. This may be particularly promising in BRAF‐ or KRAS‐driven NSCLC, where cotargeting oncogenic pathways and immune checkpoints may enhance tumor immunogenicity and improve therapeutic outcomes.
In conclusion, our findings demonstrate that specific oncogenic alterations, particularly KRAS, ERBB2, BRAF, and MET exon 14, are associated with higher PD‐L1 expression and TMB compared to EGFR‐, ALK‐, and RET‐driven tumors. TP53 mutations further enhance immunogenicity when co‐occurring with these alterations but not in EGFR‐mutated tumors. Importantly, cytology specimens consistently yielded adequate material for molecular and immune biomarker testing, which underscores their value in guiding immunotherapy decisions in NSCLC.
